nameStory: The "trailing" part of this plant's name comes from its wandering, vine-like stems that sprawl along the ground or climb over other plants. The "fuzzy-bean" name makes perfect sense once you see the soft, downy hairs covering the bean pods and leaves, giving them a velvety texture that's pleasant to touch.
description: Trailing fuzzy-bean is a sprawling annual vine with a relaxed, wandering growth habit. It produces small purple or pink pea-like flowers followed by fuzzy seed pods that contain edible beans. The plant can trail along the ground for several feet or climb up through other vegetation using its twining stems. Its three-leaflet compound leaves and fuzzy texture make it distinctive among New England's wild legumes.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, curved pods covered in soft, velvety hairs that feel pleasant to stroke - this fuzzy texture is the plant's signature feature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pea-like flowers in shades of purple, pink, or sometimes white, clustered at the ends of long stalks rising above the leaves

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-leaflet compound leaves (like a clover) with oval to lance-shaped leaflets that may have subtle hairs and feel slightly rough

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Trailing or climbing vine that sprawls along the ground or twines up through other plants, often forming loose tangles

habitat: Look for trailing fuzzy-bean in sandy soils, especially along coastlines, riverbanks, and disturbed areas. It thrives in open, sunny spots with well-drained soil and is particularly common in coastal plain areas of southern New England. You'll often find it growing among beach grasses or scrambling through low shrubs in sandy clearings.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin their sprawling growth, with the first compound leaves appearing as three-leaflet clusters.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with purple-pink pea flowers blooming from July through August, followed by the development of the characteristic fuzzy seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Mature fuzzy pods ripen and split open to release seeds, while the entire plant begins to die back as an annual.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain - seeds overwinter in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: The beans inside those fuzzy pods are actually edible and were traditionally used as food by Native Americans - they taste somewhat like lima beans when cooked, making this humble trailing vine a genuine wild food source hiding in plain sight along our beaches and roadsides.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other wild beans, but the consistently fuzzy pods are the dead giveaway - other wild legumes in our area produce smooth pods. Remember: if the pod feels like velvet, you've found fuzzy-bean!
contextualKnowledge: Also known as "annual sand bean" or "amberique-bean," this plant shows how Native American food traditions included many species we now consider just "weeds" - it's a reminder that our roadsides and wild places often contain forgotten food sources.
compareHints: Trailing fuzzy-bean differs from its relative slickseed fuzzybean primarily in its consistently hairy pods - slickseed fuzzybean has smooth pods as its name suggests. Both share the trailing habit and three-leaflet leaves, but running your finger over the pod will immediately tell you which species you've found.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Slickseed fuzzybean is the smallest and most delicate of the fuzzybean species, with thinner leaflets that are rarely lobed compared to trailing fuzzy-bean's more robust, often deeply lobed leaves.
